analysis.one_liner: Bans contracts that require workers to pay union fees as a condition of employment.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred on February 11, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to prohibit union security agreements — the contracts that let employers require workers to join a union or pay fees for union representation as a condition of employment. It would repeal those provisions in both the National Labor Relations Act, which covers most private workplaces, and the Railway Labor Act, which covers railroads and airlines. It would also strike the special provision that lets unionized construction companies sign pre-hire agreements with unions before workers are hired.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees who object to paying union dues or fees would no longer have to pay them as a condition of keeping their job. Employers would also gain, because unions would have a harder time collecting the money that funds bargaining, strikes, and grievance handling.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act that allow a union and employer to agree that employees must join the union or pay fees to keep their job [S2] [S3].
Repeals the parallel provision in the Railway Labor Act, including the rule allowing railroads to deduct union dues from paychecks as a condition of employment [S2] [S3].
Eliminates the building-and-construction provision letting unionized employers sign agreements with a union covering employees before they are hired [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would lose the fee and dues revenue from workers in union workplaces who choose not to join. Workers covered by union contracts would also bear a cost in the longer run, because weaker union financing generally means less money and leverage for negotiating wages and benefits.

drawbacks.text: Workers who stop paying but stay in the bargaining unit would still receive union-negotiated wages, benefits, and grievance representation without contributing to the cost, which unions argue undercuts the funding that makes representation possible [S2].
Striking the construction pre-hire provision would eliminate a contracting arrangement widely used in unionized construction, destabilizing existing agreements in that industry [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is framed as protecting individual workers' freedom not to support a union, and for an employee who objects to the fees, the immediate gain is real. The cost it imposes is on the institutions that fund workplace bargaining: unions would lose compulsory fee revenue, and the free-rider dynamic could gradually weaken the wages and benefits those same employees receive. It is a genuine trade-off between individual choice and collective bargaining strength, weighted by its sponsors toward individual choice and by its opponents toward union strength.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Coverdell introduced the bill in the Senate on February 11, 1999, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Thurmond, Smith of New Hampshire, Grassley, and Helms [S1] [S3].
The full Senate took only one action: reading it twice and referring it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5].
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it received no further action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and workers who rely on union security agreements kept the existing funding structure for collective bargaining, because the bill died without ever reaching the Senate floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Labor unions kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Paul Coverdell
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban union security agreements and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 23 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans; none of them were among the committee members who advanced it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral; majority controlled by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors and the sponsor were Republicans, and the bill never reached the floor, so there are no recorded votes; no Democrat is listed in support.

industries.note: The bill would cut off the fees and dues unions collect from workers who decline to join, directly reducing the money that funds bargaining, grievances, and organizing. Union representation for the workers in the unit would continue regardless, so union losses in this bill run alongside those of the employees they represent.
Without union security agreements, unions would have less assured revenue and therefore less bargaining leverage and strike capacity, which shifts power toward employers in contract negotiations.

Striking the pre-hire agreement provision would eliminate the mechanism that lets union contractors and unions set terms before workers are hired, disrupting arrangements common in that sector for both contractors and union members.
